---
name: dashboard
description: "Build or change a Bot's Dashboard tab: a page worth returning to, with real work woven into its design. dashboard_save stores it; dashboard_apply puts it live. Values arrive through declared fields, independently of the page."
triggers: dashboard, my dashboard, dashboard tab, change my dashboard, another dashboard, dashboard page, show me a different, go back to the old dashboard, build a dashboard, dashboard gallery, dashboard template
---

# The Dashboard Tab

One page per Bot. You design it, the person owns it, and the gateway feeds
its declared fields. The page, the values and the frame have different jobs:

| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| page | your HTML, CSS and script, versioned when applied |
| values | recorded facts, pushed through the declared model |
| frame | isolation, text bindings and the subscription bridge |

## 1. Save, check, apply

Read `dashboard_fields` for the page in force and its fields, and
`dashboard_types` for the available folds and row keys. Tell the person what
changed when the new page is live. Work that has grown a lot -- more workstreams, a
longer history, a new kind of reading -- is a good reason to redesign the page
once; it is never a reason to redraw it every turn.

`dashboard_save` takes `model`, `view` and an optional `theme`. `view.html`
holds the markup, CSS and script; it is the only view, and a stored view of
blocks is read back as `view.html`. Every field read by a binding or a script belongs in `model`.
The gateway derives `kind` and `bound_to` from the caller. Saving stores a
draft; `dashboard_apply` with no arguments makes it a new live version.

The save runs the page once, offline, over a synthetic copy of the current
record: the same fields, list lengths, nulls and types, with invented values.
Booleans and fixed vocabulary words are kept; an enum uses its declared labels.
Keys are kept when the page spells them out or the type catalog names them.
Nested objects inside list rows can have invented keys. Read fields by their
published names. The browser sees the copy, not the record.

The `verification` result is `passed`, `failed` with script error positions,
`timed_out`, or `skipped` with a reason. A failed page needs a repair and a new
save before apply. A count above its total can be a synthetic-data mismatch;
a missing field, null or wrong type is still a case the page needs to handle.
A pass means the first paint raised no script errors: later pushes, small
screens, visual quality and colour contrast still need their own checks.

**Look at the page.** `dashboard_snapshot` draws your applied page in the
same offline run, over your real data, and returns a PNG file path; open it
with your file-read tool. The picture is one 1280x800 view of the top of the
page, as the person's tab shows it in the default light theme, so judge what it
says as well as layout, colour, type and fit; their own theme pack or dark mode
can show other colours. The answer also prints the rendered text of the WHOLE
page, below the first screen too, between two fixed lines: check each bound
value there, and look after a field for `[not current]` (the read had no value
for it) or `[updated <age> · ...]` / `[may be out of date · ...]` (its value is
stale), in the Dashboard's language. The
text leaves out canvas drawings, form-control values and what an unfetched CDN
library would draw, and is cut at 6000 characters (the answer says so). A page
you only saved has no picture: apply it first. When the run cannot start it
answers "no image" with the reason and no file; an earlier picture is not the
page as it is now. A template page has no picture. The file and the text hold
real values: leave them where they are.

The gateway's secret filter also processes markup and script. A note reports
how many places changed and the first line, without revealing the replaced
text. A long identifier-like string can trigger it; shorter pieces joined in
code avoid accidental identifier matches. The offline check does not fetch
CDN libraries. A script that stops only because such a library is missing
returns `skipped`; other errors remain failures. One check runs at a time.
Busy or low-memory hosts skip it; the save waits at most about twelve seconds.

A template from `dashboard_templates` uses `dashboard_apply(template_id=...)`.
`dashboard_preview` is an optional look when the person asks, not an approval
gate for authored code. `dashboard_rollback` restores a version listed by
`dashboard_fields`; restoring an old version itself creates a new version.

**Progress goes on the page, not in chat.** People check a Bot once or
twice a day, and the page is what they read. Keep where your work stands on
your Dashboard page; the chat gets few reports, and when it gets one it covers
several things in one message, never a stream of small updates. No goal or
milestone is needed for a page: the first time you have work to report is
reason enough to build one.

**The daily review.** Your daily goal wake asks you to review your page:
read it against the latest data (`dashboard_fields` for each field and its
source, `dashboard_types` for the folds behind it), check that the page as a
whole still makes sense for the work you do now, and update what is stale --
a field with `dashboard_write`, the page with `dashboard_save` and
`dashboard_apply` when a section no longer fits. A page that is current stays
as it is. Then find one way to make the page better -- clearer, better made,
nicer to look at -- by sections 2 to 6 below, and make it: one small, steady
improvement a day rather than a redesign, every number still read from a fold
and none invented.

**Writing your page, and asking first on a template.** With nothing on your
Dashboard tab, having work to report, or a wake that tells you to build your
page, is the go-ahead:
write it, `dashboard_save` it and `dashboard_apply` it, then post one short
message that a Dashboard page is ready on the Dashboard tab -- no preview, no
card, and no second message. On a template page (one the user adopted, or the
page named for you) you never replace it unasked. When a Kiro Crew note in your
turn says you can offer your own page, call `offer_dashboard_page` once: it
raises one card asking whether to build a page around your goal in place of
that template, and writes nothing. If the user says yes you are woken to write,
save and apply it, with no second question, and post the same one message. If they say no,
or the card expires, nothing changes and you are not asked again. A page the
user asks for in chat needs no card: write it then.

Only the owner writes its page or values. A worker reports through
`work_report`, whose record feeds the owner's folds.

## 2. A page worth returning to

Aim for a page the person enjoys opening, even before reading a number.
Its whole composition and the way the work appears within it create that
appeal. Clear data and a distinctive visual character belong together.

**Make the design your own.** Carry the user's chosen style through later
changes. When they leave the style open, choose a coherent direction from
the work and its context. That freedom includes a theme, atmosphere and
visual metaphor, as well as an abstract design. Let that character reach
across the page rather than stop at a heading or an icon.

**Themed pages are an option.** `THEMES.md` beside this file holds
whole-page theme ideas, such as an arcade cabinet, a cork board or a
departure board. When the person leaves the style open, you may pick one
that suits the work; most people do not know a theme is possible. When they
ask what looks are possible, name two or three. A clean, plain page is just
as correct, and a theme is never required. When one is used, it changes
only the look: every value stays bound to its fold and every link keeps
working.

**Give the whole page visual depth.** Backgrounds, wallpaper, pattern,
texture, expressive frames and layered surfaces are welcome parts of the
design. Their purpose can be atmosphere rather than measurement. Give the
data equal care: its placement, scale and visual form belong to the same
composition. A decorative layer can enrich the work without pretending to
be evidence about it.

**Let the evidence suggest the picture.** Look for change, comparison,
proportion, relationships and progress in what the page can actually read.
Charts reveal recorded changes over time; comparisons and distributions
can reveal a great deal from current values alone. Progress draws on a
known target or a defined total. A state without a measure can still have
a vivid visual presence and motion that means active, waiting or finished.
Choose the form that helps this work make sense, with detail available
where it is useful. A count can be part of a larger picture as well as a
readable number. A distribution of worker states is a measured comparison,
not a claim that each worker has completed a fraction of its task.

**Make it feel alive.** Subtle ambient motion and animation run constantly
while the page is in view, not only when a value changes, and lift the whole
experience. Data-driven motion on top helps the reader notice an arrival, a
change or a finish. Give those two
kinds of motion a clear purpose and a shared rhythm. Keep long-running
effects light on resources, without repeated layout work, and pause them
while the page is hidden. The still composition keeps its character and
meaning.

**Reduced motion is for the reader who set it.** Under
`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` every value jumps to its target, ambient
layers hold still and no entrance plays; the page still answers input.
Every other reader gets the motion, so do not hold it back by default.

**Keep every claim true.** Numbers, labels and data-driven geometry agree
with their sources and with each other. Proportions have a stated meaning
and a real denominator. Time charts show recorded samples and their time
range. Missing readings, incomplete history and unmeasured progress stay
distinct from zero. Running or idle alone says nothing about how much of
a task is complete. Decoration remains distinct from measured evidence,
and an animation's intermediate positions are not new measurements.

**Make the work easy to read.** Use plain words and useful names, keeping
internal ids, session keys and file-system paths out of the visible page.
Map each phase, state and event type to its meaning; an unknown type gets a
truthful general phrase. Free text an agent wrote into a fold -- a ledger's
`next`, a report's summary, a waiting item's text -- can carry a session name,
a path or a whole build report: show it as a short plain sentence (its first
sentence, the rest behind a disclosure), with ids and paths left out. Important changes and things waiting on the person remain easy
to find. Colour works with words or shape to carry meaning. Decorative
layers leave text and useful controls clear, and long content fits from
a narrow view to a wide one: at 320px a label and its value wrap or stack,
and nothing is clipped or scrolls sideways.

**Design colour as a whole.** The tab's theme variables are a useful base;
custom variables, textures and independently coloured surfaces can also
belong to the design. Pair each surface with text that reads on it, and
check the complete result in both light and dark. Treat a colour warning
as a place to inspect and improve, rather than a reason to remove the
page's character.

**Pair type, do not name it.** The frame gives three role variables,
`var(--font-sans)`, `var(--font-serif)` and `var(--font-mono)`, each built
from generic families so every system draws its own face. Use at most two
families on a page, each with a clear job: one that reads, for headings and
body, and one for numbers, code or ids. Monospace is for code, ids and
aligned figures, never for body text or headings. Build hierarchy with
size, weight and colour, not with another family; `font-variant-numeric:
tabular-nums` aligns figures without switching to monospace. Text in any
one script stays in one style; the generic families already pick each
script's system face. A style the user names wins.

Judge the result both as a whole picture and as a view of the work. It
should remain worth looking at when the values hold still, and make a
real change in the work easy to see when they move. A tidy set of numbers
alone does not establish that quality.

## 3. What a glance should answer

The page has both visual character and a useful view of the work:

| Question | Available evidence |
|---|---|
| Where does the work stand? | work items, workstreams, relevant goal readings |
| What is running right now? | workers, workstreams, helpers in this session |
| What is stuck? | blocked work, failed helpers, outstanding dependencies |
| What needs me? | waiting items and approvals |

Anything waiting on the person is easy to find, never hidden. When nothing
waits, the page says so. Include `waiting.count` and `waiting.items` in the
model so a request arriving after the first paint is visible too. Choose
vocabulary that keeps worker sessions,
accepted work items and project outcomes distinct. A closed session does not
establish that its task was accepted. Decisions use the real `ask_question`
and approval surfaces; a drawn control carries no approval authority.

## 4. Choose evidence before drawing it

The page presents recorded facts rather than becoming a second status store.
Fold-backed fields update by themselves. Choose evidence that explains this
project, including relevant goals and milestones when they reveal progress;
repeating the Profile form is different from drawing a useful project view.

**Reply buttons.** A button you draw can offer the reader a reply. Post
`parent.postMessage({type: 'kirocrew-dashboard:act', text}, '*')` to put `text`
in the reader's chat box; they press send. Post `type: 'kirocrew-dashboard:send'`
to send it into this crewmate's own chat in one click. `send` is only a request:
the host sends it only after a recent real interaction with the window while your page
holds focus, never to a target you name, at most once every few seconds, and it falls back to `act` when the reader
switched one-click sends off on the Profile tab or when the chat is busy or
waiting on an approval or a question. The text is trimmed, at most 600 characters,
with no control characters but a newline. When a reply arrives it begins
`[Dashboard card]`: the reader clicked one of the replies you offered. It is not
an approval of a tool call or permission and does not answer an open question,
and the tools Kiro Crew gates ask the reader first while you answer it, even in a chat
that otherwise trusts your tools (a tool your own agent file pre-allows is not gated
here and runs as usual). You cannot hand work on from that turn (no
sub-agent, other session, workflow, task, cron job or loop); ask the reader to request it
in the chat.
Keep `act` for replies that need the reader's edit before they go.

| Evidence | Fold and shape |
|---|---|
| worker sessions and current states | `workers.items`, `counts`, `total`, `omitted` |
| work items and their outcomes | `work`, `workstreams.items` |
| hourly accepted work and measured spend | `workstreams.series`: `hour`, `accepted`, `credits` |
| parallel work and task spans | each workstream's `tasks`: `created_at`, `closed_at`, `status` |
| goal readings and milestone counts | `goal.milestones` (`target`, `current`), `milestones_total` |
| recent recorded events | `timeline.moments`: `time`, `type`, optional event details |
| things waiting on the person | `waiting.items`, `count`; `approvals` |
| helpers, tool use and spend of the live session, since it started | `subagents`, `tools`, `usage` |
| the latest result a script cron bound to you recorded | `custom.latest.<type>.data`, `at`, `writer` |

`dashboard_types` publishes paths, `row_keys`, `names_the_row` and nested row
hints. A path ends at an array: bind the whole array and read its rows in
script. Array length is a useful derived count, not the only possible binding.
A map is read by its published keys. `folded_through` reports how far a fold
has consumed its log; it is not a sample count or proof of nonempty data.

`workers` has states, not per-worker completion percentages. `goal` keeps a
latest snapshot: its `target` and `current` strings may be prose rather than
numbers. Show each milestone's reading beside its target, as text. Whether a
milestone is reached is what you recorded in its reading with
`key_result_progress` ("met", "done", a number), never something the page
works out; an arbitrary prose target is not a denominator. With no milestones confirmed, show that state rather
than a 0/0 ratio. A goal's text can carry a repository path: show the project
by its name, and a source by the file's name within the project, never an
absolute or home-directory path. A source list can lag a newer measurement: resolve differences against
the actual project before presenting an old issue as still open.
`workstreams` is the measured project history a page most often misses: each
board's `accepted` of `total`, its `tasks` with their spans, and `series`, hourly
buckets of accepted items and recorded spend -- a bounded set, not guaranteed
continuous history. `usage`, `tools`, `timeline` and `subagents` describe the
live session only, from when it last started; spend across the project is each
workstream's `credits`, with `credits_reported` false where nothing was measured. Lists expose omitted counts; retain that
meaning when drawing a subset. Unreported spend differs from measured zero.

`custom` is what a script cron bound to you feeds without a model turn: each
`ctx.crew_log_append(type, data)` call lands as the latest record under
`custom.latest.<type>`, with the script's `data`, its ISO `at` and the `writer`
(`cron:<job id>`) the gateway stamped. Bind `custom.latest.<type>.data.<key>` for
a cell, or the whole `data` object for a script to draw. The record is the
script's own words: draw it as text, and show its `at` so a stale poll reads as
stale. Only a cron bound to you can write here, and it can never name who wrote.

A record is not current just because it is the latest. Have the script pass
`max_age_s` (about twice its interval) to `ctx.crew_log_append`; the row then
carries `stale_after`, the gateway's write time plus that. When the job's run
fails, the gateway adds `failed_at` and `last_error` to each record that job
wrote, and lists the job in `custom.failures` even when it never landed a record.
Bind the row, not only its `data`, and draw it as stale or failed, never as
current, when `failed_at` is present or `Date.now()` is past `stale_after`. A
record exactly at `stale_after` is still current. Both marks clear only when
the job writes again, so a job that writes only on change stays marked failed
until its next change; write each run if the page must show recovery.

For a project fact absent from folds, first look for its recording tool or an
existing project artifact. An agentic field can hold a verified snapshot as a
number, text, boolean, array or object, as well as your own verdict. Label its
source and observation time visibly, and use `dashboard_write` when that
source changes. A snapshot remains an observation at that time, not a claim
of automatic freshness. Repeated observations can form a measured series;
values invented for the sake of a chart cannot. The save reply names
`manual_fields`, and the frame marks agent-written claims.

## 5. The frame contract

The page is a body fragment in a gateway-owned iframe. Inline CSS, SVG and JS
can draw it. Network access is closed: `connect-src 'none'`; no fetch, XHR,
websocket, remote fonts or beacons. Libraries are limited to the frame's fixed
allowlist. Embedded imagery is an inline `data:` URL, in `view.html` or in
`theme.css`; `theme.css` refuses a `url()` with an address, which would load
nothing. A page cannot loosen the frame policy.

Read `references/frame-contract.md` (next to this file) before you write a
page's script, data bindings or missing-value handling: what the frame runs,
what it refuses, and how a page shows a value it does not have.

## 6. Theme and reach

The frame supplies `--bg`, `--bg-elevated`, `--card`, `--card-fg`, `--text`,
`--text-strong`, `--muted`, `--border`, `--accent`, `--accent-subtle`, `--ok`,
`--warn`, `--danger` and other host theme variables. Your CSS and `theme.tokens`
can define custom properties too. An undefined variable uses its fallback;
a defined custom variable is a normal design tool. The frame marks its scheme
on the body as `data-mode="light"` or `data-mode="dark"`; a Tailwind `dark:`
utility and a `[data-mode=dark]` selector read it. No host element carries a
class, so every class name is the page's own, `light` and `dark` included.

Pair surface and text colours, either through host variables or your own
scheme-aware definitions. Fixed colours can also form a readable self-contained
surface when its text is designed with it. A fallback in `var(--text, ...)`
is unused while the tab defines `--text`: that text still changes with the
host scheme. A fixed surface can instead pair with its own text property,
including captions, bound cells and chart labels. The save's theme warnings
are CSS heuristics, not measured contrast failures. Inspect the named surface
in both schemes while preserving the intended design.

A page fits from 320px through an expanded view, with wrapping or disclosure
for dense detail. A banner has space without covering data. A link to a web
page or a dashboard path (`/chat?sid=...`) uses `target="_blank"
rel="noopener noreferrer"`; the host opens it after the person's click, a web
page in a new tab and a dashboard page in place.
Data-driven changes stay readable
while ambient layers give the page continuity. When a bound value moves or a
new item lands, the `living-ui` skill says how that motion should feel. Skip
the idle tour it describes for explainers: this page stays open all day.

## 7. Pages to start from

`gallery/` and `GALLERY.md` beside this file show how a page declares and binds
its fields, not how a page should look. Read a package for the connection you
need, then compose the page for this work. Its plain appearance is a wiring
example, not a quality target. Your model declares every field your script or
markup reads; the controller pushes only that list.

Search documentation with `search_docs` and locate controls with `find_ui`
when a fold, field or setting needs clarification.

and none invented.

**Writing your page, and asking first on a template.** With nothing on your
Dashboard tab, having work to report, or a wake that tells you to build your
page, is the go-ahead:
write it, `dashboard_save` it and `dashboard_apply` it, then post one short
message that a Dashboard page is ready on the Dashboard tab -- no preview, no
card, and no second message. On a template page (one the user adopted, or the
page named for you) you never replace it unasked. When a Kiro Crew note in your
turn says you can offer your own page, call `offer_dashboard_page` once: it
raises one card asking whether to build a page around your goal in place of
that template, and writes nothing. If the user says yes you are woken to write,
save and apply it, with no second question, and post the same one message. If they say no,
or the card expires, nothing changes and you are not asked again. A page the
user asks for in chat needs no card: write it then.

Only the owner writes its page or values. A worker reports through
`work_report`, whose record feeds the owner's folds.

## 2. A page worth returning to

Aim for a page the person enjoys opening, even before reading a number.
Its whole composition and the way the work appears within it create that
appeal. Clear data and a distinctive visual character belong together.

**Make the design your own.** Carry the user's chosen style through later
changes. When they leave the style open, choose a coherent direction from
the work and its context. That freedom includes a theme, atmosphere and
visual metaphor, as well as an abstract design. Let that character reach
across the page rather than stop at a heading or an icon.

**Themed pages are an option.** `THEMES.md` beside this file holds
whole-page theme ideas, such as an arcade cabinet, a cork board or a
departure board. When the person leaves the style open, you may pick one
that suits the work; most people do not know a theme is possible. When they
ask what looks are possible, name two or three. A clean, plain page is just
as correct, and a theme is never required. When one is used, it changes
only the look: every value stays bound to its fold and every link keeps
working.

**Give the whole page visual depth.** Backgrounds, wallpaper, pattern,
texture, expressive frames and layered surfaces are welcome parts of the
design. Their purpose can be atmosphere rather than measurement. Give the
data equal care: its placement, scale and visual form belong to the same
composition. A decorative layer can enrich the work without pretending to
be evidence about it.

**Let the evidence suggest the picture.** Look for change, comparison,
proportion, relationships and progress in what the page can actually read.
Charts reveal recorded changes over time; comparisons and distributions
can reveal a great deal from current values alone. Progress draws on a
known target or a defined total. A state without a measure can still have
a vivid visual presence and motion that means active, waiting or finished.
Choose the form that helps this work make sense, with detail available
where it is useful. A count can be part of a larger picture as well as a
readable number. A distribution of worker states is a measured comparison,
not a claim that each worker has completed a fraction of its task.

**Make it feel alive.** Subtle ambient motion and animation run constantly
while the page is in view, not only when a value changes, and lift the whole
experience. Data-driven motion on top helps the reader notice an arrival, a
change or a finish. Give those two
kinds of motion a clear purpose and a shared rhythm. Keep long-running
effects light on resources, without repeated layout work, and pause them
while the page is hidden. The still composition keeps its character and
meaning.

**Reduced motion is for the reader who set it.** Under
`prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` every value jumps to its target, ambient
layers hold still and no entrance plays; the page still answers input.
Every other reader gets the motion, so do not hold it back by default.

**Keep every claim true.** Numbers, labels and data-driven geometry agree
with their sources and with each other. Proportions have a stated meaning
and a real denominator. Time charts show recorded samples and their time
range. Missing readings, incomplete history and unmeasured progress stay
distinct from zero. Running or idle alone says nothing about how much of
a task is complete. Decoration remains distinct from measured evidence,
and an animation's intermediate positions are not new measurements.

**Make the work easy to read.** Use plain words and useful names, keeping
internal ids, session keys and file-system paths out of the visible page.
Map each phase, state and event type to its meaning; an unknown type gets a
truthful general phrase. Free text an agent wrote into a fold -- a ledger's
`next`, a report's summary, a waiting item's text -- can carry a session name,
a path or a whole build report: show it as a short plain sentence (its first
sentence, the rest behind a disclosure), with ids and paths left out. Important changes and things waiting on the person remain easy
to find. Colour works with words or shape to carry meaning. Decorative
layers leave text and useful controls clear, and long content fits from
a narrow view to a wide one: at 320px a label and its value wrap or stack,
and nothing is clipped or scrolls sideways.

**Design colour as a whole.** The tab's theme variables are a useful base;
custom variables, textures and independently coloured surfaces can also
belong to the design. Pair each surface with text that reads on it, and
check the complete result in both light and dark. Treat a colour warning
as a place to inspect and improve, rather than a reason to remove the
page's character.

**Pair type, do not name it.** The frame gives three role variables,
`var(--font-sans)`, `var(--font-serif)` and `var(--font-mono)`, each built
from generic families so every system draws its own face. Use at most two
families on a page, each with a clear job: one that reads, for headings and
body, and one for numbers, code or ids. Monospace is for code, ids and
aligned figures, never for body text or headings. Build hierarchy with
size, weight and colour, not with another family; `font-variant-numeric:
tabular-nums` aligns figures without switching to monospace. Text in any
one script stays in one style; the generic families already pick each
script's system face. A style the user names wins.

Judge the result both as a whole picture and as a view of the work. It
should remain worth looking at when the values hold still, and make a
real change in the work easy to see when they move. A tidy set of numbers
alone does not establish that quality.

## 3. What a glance should answer

The page has both visual character and a useful view of the work:

| Question | Available evidence |
|---|---|
| Where does the work stand? | work items, workstreams, relevant goal readings |
| What is running right now? | workers, workstreams, helpers in this session |
| What is stuck? | blocked work, failed helpers, outstanding dependencies |
| What needs me? | waiting items and approvals |

Anything waiting on the person is easy to find, never hidden. When nothing
waits, the page says so. Include `waiting.count` and `waiting.items` in the
model so a request arriving after the first paint is visible too. Choose
vocabulary that keeps worker sessions,
accepted work items and project outcomes distinct. A closed session does not
establish that its task was accepted. Decisions use the real `ask_question`
and approval surfaces; a drawn control carries no approval authority.

## 4. Choose evidence before drawing it

The page presents recorded facts rather than becoming a second status store.
Fold-backed fields update by themselves. Choose evidence that explains this
project, including relevant goals and milestones when they reveal progress;
repeating the Profile form is different from drawing a useful project view.

**Reply buttons.** A button you draw can offer the reader a reply. Post
`parent.postMessage({type: 'kirocrew-dashboard:act', text}, '*')` to put `text`
in the reader's chat box; they press send. Post `type: 'kirocrew-dashboard:send'`
to send it into this crewmate's own chat in one click. `send` is only a request:
the host sends it only after a recent real interaction with the window while your page
holds focus, never to a target you name, at most once every few seconds, and it falls back to `act` when the reader
switched one-click sends off on the Profile tab or when the chat is busy or
waiting on an approval or a question. The text is trimmed, at most 600 characters,
with no control characters but a newline. When a reply arrives it begins
`[Dashboard card]`: the reader clicked one of the replies you offered. It is not
an approval of a tool call or permission and does not answer an open question,
and the tools Kiro Crew gates ask the reader first while you answer it, even in a chat
that otherwise trusts your tools (a tool your own agent file pre-allows is not gated
here and runs as usual). You cannot hand work on from that turn (no
sub-agent, other session, workflow, task, cron job or loop); ask the reader to request it
in the chat.
Keep `act` for replies that need the reader's edit before they go.

| Evidence | Fold and shape |
|---|---|
| worker sessions and current states | `workers.items`, `counts`, `total`, `omitted` |
| work items and their outcomes | `work`, `workstreams.items` |
| hourly accepted work and measured spend | `workstreams.series`: `hour`, `accepted`, `credits` |
| parallel work and task spans | each workstream's `tasks`: `created_at`, `closed_at`, `status` |
| goal readings and milestone counts | `goal.milestones` (`target`, `current`), `milestones_total` |
| recent recorded events | `timeline.moments`: `time`, `type`, optional event details |
| things waiting on the person | `waiting.items`, `count`; `approvals` |
| helpers, tool use and spend of the live session, since it started | `subagents`, `tools`, `usage` |
| the latest result a script cron bound to you recorded | `custom.latest.<type>.data`, `at`, `writer` |

`dashboard_types` publishes paths, `row_keys`, `names_the_row` and nested row
hints. A path ends at an array: bind the whole array and read its rows in
script. Array length is a useful derived count, not the only possible binding.
A map is read by its published keys. `folded_through` reports how far a fold
has consumed its log; it is not a sample count or proof of nonempty data.

`workers` has states, not per-worker completion percentages. `goal` keeps a
latest snapshot: its `target` and `current` strings may be prose rather than
numbers. Show each milestone's reading beside its target, as text. Whether a
milestone is reached is what you recorded in its reading with
`key_result_progress` ("met", "done", a number), never something the page
works out; an arbitrary prose target is not a denominator. With no milestones confirmed, show that state rather
than a 0/0 ratio. A goal's text can carry a repository path: show the project
by its name, and a source by the file's name within the project, never an
absolute or home-directory path. A source list can lag a newer measurement: resolve differences against
the actual project before presenting an old issue as still open.
`workstreams` is the measured project history a page most often misses: each
board's `accepted` of `total`, its `tasks` with their spans, and `series`, hourly
buckets of accepted items and recorded spend -- a bounded set, not guaranteed
continuous history. `usage`, `tools`, `timeline` and `subagents` describe the
live session only, from when it last started; spend across the project is each
workstream's `credits`, with `credits_reported` false where nothing was measured. Lists expose omitted counts; retain that
meaning when drawing a subset. Unreported spend differs from measured zero.

`custom` is what a script cron bound to you feeds without a model turn: each
`ctx.crew_log_append(type, data)` call lands as the latest record under
`custom.latest.<type>`, with the script's `data`, its ISO `at` and the `writer`
(`cron:<job id>`) the gateway stamped. Bind `custom.latest.<type>.data.<key>` for
a cell, or the whole `data` object for a script to draw. The record is the
script's own words: draw it as text, and show its `at` so a stale poll reads as
stale. Only a cron bound to you can write here, and it can never name who wrote.

A record is not current just because it is the latest. Have the script pass
`max_age_s` (about twice its interval) to `ctx.crew_log_append`; the row then
carries `stale_after`, the gateway's write time plus that. When the job's run
fails, the gateway adds `failed_at` and `last_error` to each record that job
wrote, and lists the job in `custom.failures` even when it never landed a record.
Bind the row, not only its `data`, and draw it as stale or failed, never as
current, when `failed_at` is present or `Date.now()` is past `stale_after`. A
record exactly at `stale_after` is still current. Both marks clear only when
the job writes again, so a job that writes only on change stays marked failed
until its next change; write each run if the page must show recovery.

For a project fact absent from folds, first look for its recording tool or an
existing project artifact. An agentic field can hold a verified snapshot as a
number, text, boolean, array or object, as well as your own verdict. Label its
source and observation time visibly, and use `dashboard_write` when that
source changes. A snapshot remains an observation at that time, not a claim
of automatic freshness. Repeated observations can form a measured series;
values invented for the sake of a chart cannot. The save reply names
`manual_fields`, and the frame marks agent-written claims.

## 5. The frame contract

The page is a body fragment in a gateway-owned iframe. Inline CSS, SVG and JS
can draw it. Network access is closed: `connect-src 'none'`; no fetch, XHR,
websocket, remote fonts or beacons. Libraries are limited to the frame's fixed
allowlist. Embedded imagery is an inline `data:` URL, in `view.html` or in
`theme.css`; `theme.css` refuses a `url()` with an address, which would load
nothing. A page cannot loosen the frame policy.

Read `references/frame-contract.md` (next to this file) before you write a
page's script, data bindings or missing-value handling: what the frame runs,
what it refuses, and how a page shows a value it does not have.

## 6. Theme and reach

The frame supplies `--bg`, `--bg-elevated`, `--card`, `--card-fg`, `--text`,
`--text-strong`, `--muted`, `--border`, `--accent`, `--accent-subtle`, `--ok`,
`--warn`, `--danger` and other host theme variables. Your CSS and `theme.tokens`
can define custom properties too. An undefined variable uses its fallback;
a defined custom variable is a normal design tool. The frame marks its scheme
on the body as `data-mode="light"` or `data-mode="dark"`; a Tailwind `dark:`
utility and a `[data-mode=dark]` selector read it. No host element carries a
class, so every class name is the page's own, `light` and `dark` included.

Pair surface and text colours, either through host variables or your own
scheme-aware definitions. Fixed colours can also form a readable self-contained
surface when its text is designed with it. A fallback in `var(--text, ...)`
is unused while the tab defines `--text`: that text still changes with the
host scheme. A fixed surface can instead pair with its own text property,
including captions, bound cells and chart labels. The save's theme warnings
are CSS heuristics, not measured contrast failures. Inspect the named surface
in both schemes while preserving the intended design.

A page fits from 320px through an expanded view, with wrapping or disclosure
for dense detail. A banner has space without covering data. A link to a web
page or a dashboard path (`/chat?sid=...`) uses `target="_blank"
rel="noopener noreferrer"`; the host opens it after the person's click, a web
page in a new tab and a dashboard page in place.
Data-driven changes stay readable
while ambient layers give the page continuity. When a bound value moves or a
new item lands, the `living-ui` skill says how that motion should feel. Skip
the idle tour it describes for explainers: this page stays open all day.

## 7. Pages to start from

`gallery/` and `GALLERY.md` beside this file show how a page declares and binds
its fields, not how a page should look. Read a package for the connection you
need, then compose the page for this work. Its plain appearance is a wiring
example, not a quality target. Your model declares every field your script or
markup reads; the controller pushes only that list.

Search documentation with `search_docs` and locate controls with `find_ui`
when a fold, field or setting needs clarification.

# Reading the kirocrew-debug tools

Five read-only tools answer five questions about the live gateway. The tool
descriptions say what each one covers, and `docs/reference/debug/README.md` carries
the rest. This skill is the part neither of them has: which question to ask first,
and how to read an answer without drawing the opposite conclusion.

Where the surrounding material lives, all in one reference doc. An installed build
does not carry the repository's docs tree, so read it at
[Debugging a running gateway](https://github.com/kirodotdev/KiroCrew/blob/main/docs/reference/debug/README.md),
or at `docs/reference/debug/README.md` in a checkout:

- symptom table: section "Symptom to tool"
- the sandbox traps, including the empty placeholder mounts: section "Sandbox traps"
- who may take each reading: section "Authorization"
- why the server is opt-in, and how to grant it: the paragraph above the five questions

## Ask before you conclude

1. **Before reporting that a change did not work, call `debug_gateway`.** A gateway
   that started before your commit is executing the previous revision, and a daemon
   that outlived the change hands out backends built from the old checkout. Both look
   exactly like a broken fix.
2. **A refusal is `blocked-by-policy`'s job**; `debug_refusals` gives it the class.
3. **Before calling a refused path protected, read that class.** Only
   `sensitive_path_match` means the path is protected. `unverifiable_path` means the
   path was never judged, and the row's own `action` line says what to do.

## Fields that read as the opposite of what they mean

### debug_gateway

`gateway_predates_head` has three readings, not two. `null` is neither true nor
false: the start time comes from procfs, so it is absent off Linux, and HEAD's commit
time needs a git checkout, so it is absent on an installed wheel. Treat `null` as
unmeasured and say so, rather than concluding the gateway is current.

`mcp_gateway_daemon.matches_this_install` false has two meanings, so read `fingerprint`
beside it. A real fingerprint that differs means the daemon is serving backends built
from another checkout, and a directive tool can report success against one.
`unknown (pre-fingerprint build)` means the daemon cannot be compared at all, which is
unmeasured rather than stale. A null `matches_this_install` has two causes, told apart
by `running` beside it: `running: false` is a measured absence (no daemon), while
`running: null` is a FAILED probe — the daemon could not be described — which is
unmeasured, not a confirmed absence. Do not read a failed probe as "no daemon".
`recorder.available` false means the build carries no diagnostics package, which is
also why three of the five tools cannot answer on it.

Either stale reading is fixed by restarting that component, which is the user's step.
Name which one is stale and hand it over rather than re-testing the change.

### debug_refusals

`self` widens to the sessions you spawned only when your caller class may read past
your own rows. An unattended, app-owned, incognito, temporary, channel-linked or
channel-mirrored caller is narrowed to its own rows instead of being refused, so a
short answer there is the scope, not an absence.

`truncated` true means the answer was cut, and it does not say by which limit.
`returned` and `scanned_bytes` do not settle it either, because they overlap: one live
log segment larger than the scan budget is read whole, so the row cap and the byte cap
can both have fired on the same answer. Asking again with a larger `last` is worth one
try, but the route clamps `last` to its own cap, so once `returned` stops growing you
have every row this tool will give. Treat a refusal you cannot see as unknown rather
than absent.

`by_class` is the histogram worth reading first. A pile of `unverifiable_path` is
resolver contention rather than policy. `live.available` false is expected and is not
a fault.

### debug_threads

`mode=now` ships an `interpretation` string that names the explanation its two numbers
support. Read that string rather than ranking the raw columns yourself. Kernel columns
are `null` off Linux, which is an absence of measurement and not a zero.

`mode=sample` only profiles when profiling is switched on: the sampler is gated on
`KIROCREW_DEBUG=1` in the GATEWAY process's own environment, which a tool call cannot
set. Otherwise the answer is a `refused` field, and that field is the shape for every
refusal here, not only for a second concurrent run. Read its message before anything
else; only the concurrent case is worth waiting out.

`deep=true` never runs py-spy, and on a default install it has no py-spy to name: the
tool ships in the optional `perf` extra, so the answer is `available: false` carrying the
reason. Where py-spy is installed the answer is the py-spy `--gil` argv with
`executed: false`, because that capture is a ptrace attach and the gateway does not spawn
its own tracer, so hand that command to the user to run.

### debug_processes

It answers identity and shape first. `cpu_pct` and `runq_wait_pct` are deltas against
the route's previous read, so the first read, a read under 1s after the last one, and
a read more than 300s after it carry `null` (with the reason in `degraded`), and
`gil_saturated_hint` is false whenever the rate is missing. `null` there is unmeasured,
not idle. Take a contention question to `debug_threads` `mode=now`.

`owner` is a label, not a session key. Through this route it reads `gateway:<pid>` or
`runtime:<pid>`, which says which gateway tracks the process or which tracked runtime it
hangs off, so do not report it as the session that owns the process. `kind` depends on
that label in one place: a subagent runtime is the same binary as a chat runtime, so
with no session label to separate them it appears as `chat`.

Nothing here kills anything. Reaping stays with the reaper, so report the pid, its kind
and its `owner` label as it is written.

### debug_snapshots

Start with `events_only=true`: the event rows are the ones that explain a moment, and
the series is what you widen to when they do not. `stats` covers every row in the
window even when the page was cut, so its extremes are true. `truncated` true hands
you a `cursor`.

## Reading a refusal from these tools

| Status | `code` | What it means | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 403 | `forbidden` | Several refusals share this code, so read the message. It covers a caller class that holds no host-wide view, a session the gateway cannot name at all, a request from another component, and a named session outside your scope | Never retry and never look for another route. Only for the host-wide-view refusal do the owner's own tab and `session=self` help; an unnameable session reads nothing, including its own rows, and an out-of-scope session key is refused however it is asked |
| 501 | `diag_unavailable` | The build carries no `kiro_crew.diag`, so threads, processes and snapshots cannot answer. Relayed verbatim so it cannot be mistaken for an empty answer | Report the build. `debug_gateway` and `debug_refusals` still work; do not synthesize the missing reading |
| 404 | `dump_missing` | A dump named by an earlier listing rotated away before this read | Re-list and read a current name |
| 503 | `dump_unreadable` | A dump named by an earlier listing is still present but could not be read (an `OSError` opening it) | Re-list; if it persists the dump is damaged, so pick another name |
| 400 | `bad_range` | An argument is malformed: an unparsable `around`, a `radius` like `5x`, a non-integer `last`, a non-finite `seconds` | Fix the argument and call again |

More codes appear. `recorder_off` (422) means the recorder is not running, so
the series has no rows. `unavailable` means nothing answered at all, which is a
transport failure rather than a refusal. `too_large` and `truncated_to_fit` mean the
answer outgrew its size budget, and `truncated_hint` states that budget and the remedy.
`dump_unreadable` (503) means a dump exists but could not be read. An argument the tool's
schema rejects (a non-integer `last`, a `mode` outside the enum) comes back as plain
`Error: <field>: ...` text with no `code`; fix the argument.

## If the tools are not there

The server is opt-in, so absence means it was not granted to this agent: say so, point
at the two halves a grant needs, the `kirocrew-debug` entry in the agent's `mcpServers`
and the `@kirocrew-debug` reference in its `tools`, and do not shell around it.

### debug_threads

`mode=now` ships an `interpretation` string that names the explanation its two numbers
support. Read that string rather than ranking the raw columns yourself. Kernel columns
are `null` off Linux, which is an absence of measurement and not a zero.

`mode=sample` only profiles when profiling is switched on: the sampler is gated on
`KIROCREW_DEBUG=1` in the GATEWAY process's own environment, which a tool call cannot
set. Otherwise the answer is a `refused` field, and that field is the shape for every
refusal here, not only for a second concurrent run. Read its message before anything
else; only the concurrent case is worth waiting out.

`deep=true` never runs py-spy, and on a default install it has no py-spy to name: the
tool ships in the optional `perf` extra, so the answer is `available: false` carrying the
reason. Where py-spy is installed the answer is the py-spy `--gil` argv with
`executed: false`, because that capture is a ptrace attach and the gateway does not spawn
its own tracer, so hand that command to the user to run.

### debug_processes

It answers identity and shape first. `cpu_pct` and `runq_wait_pct` are deltas against
the route's previous read, so the first read, a read under 1s after the last one, and
a read more than 300s after it carry `null` (with the reason in `degraded`), and
`gil_saturated_hint` is false whenever the rate is missing. `null` there is unmeasured,
not idle. Take a contention question to `debug_threads` `mode=now`.

`owner` is a label, not a session key. Through this route it reads `gateway:<pid>` or
`runtime:<pid>`, which says which gateway tracks the process or which tracked runtime it
hangs off, so do not report it as the session that owns the process. `kind` depends on
that label in one place: a subagent runtime is the same binary as a chat runtime, so
with no session label to separate them it appears as `chat`.

Nothing here kills anything. Reaping stays with the reaper, so report the pid, its kind
and its `owner` label as it is written.

### debug_snapshots

Start with `events_only=true`: the event rows are the ones that explain a moment, and
the series is what you widen to when they do not. `stats` covers every row in the
window even when the page was cut, so its extremes are true. `truncated` true hands
you a `cursor`.

## Reading a refusal from these tools

| Status | `code` | What it means | Next action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 403 | `forbidden` | Several refusals share this code, so read the message. It covers a caller class that holds no host-wide view, a session the gateway cannot name at all, a request from another component, and a named session outside your scope | Never retry and never look for another route. Only for the host-wide-view refusal do the owner's own tab and `session=self` help; an unnameable session reads nothing, including its own rows, and an out-of-scope session key is refused however it is asked |
| 501 | `diag_unavailable` | The build carries no `kiro_crew.diag`, so threads, processes and snapshots cannot answer. Relayed verbatim so it cannot be mistaken for an empty answer | Report the build. `debug_gateway` and `debug_refusals` still work; do not synthesize the missing reading |
| 404 | `dump_missing` | A dump named by an earlier listing rotated away before this read | Re-list and read a current name |
| 503 | `dump_unreadable` | A dump named by an earlier listing is still present but could not be read (an `OSError` opening it) | Re-list; if it persists the dump is damaged, so pick another name |
| 400 | `bad_range` | An argument is malformed: an unparsable `around`, a `radius` like `5x`, a non-integer `last`, a non-finite `seconds` | Fix the argument and call again |

More codes appear. `recorder_off` (422) means the recorder is not running, so
the series has no rows. `unavailable` means nothing answered at all, which is a
transport failure rather than a refusal. `too_large` and `truncated_to_fit` mean the
answer outgrew its size budget, and `truncated_hint` states that budget and the remedy.
`dump_unreadable` (503) means a dump exists but could not be read. An argument the tool's
schema rejects (a non-integer `last`, a `mode` outside the enum) comes back as plain
`Error: <field>: ...` text with no `code`; fix the argument.

## If the tools are not there

The server is opt-in, so absence means it was not granted to this agent: say so, point
at the two halves a grant needs, the `kirocrew-debug` entry in the agent's `mcpServers`
and the `@kirocrew-debug` reference in its `tools`, and do not shell around it.

---
name: explain-for
description: Explain a topic, code, error or design decision for one named audience (a 5-year-old, a manager, a designer, a grad student, a parent). Resolves who it is for, pins the ground truth first, then tunes vocabulary, analogy, tone and depth to that audience. Use when an audience is named.
triggers: explain like i am, explain like im, explain like a, explain to my, break down for, dumb it down, simplify this for, in plain english
---

# explain-for — write it for one named audience

One explanation cannot serve everyone. This skill makes you name the audience
first, verify the facts second, and only then write.

## Step 0 — check that this is actually an audience request

You reach this skill from its index entry, or — when `skills.max_triggered` is
above its default of 0 — from word-overlap against the trigger phrases above.
Either route is probabilistic and will sometimes land on a request that merely
contains the word "explain". Before entering the skill, confirm the user wants
an explanation **pitched at somebody**. If they just want to know why CI
failed, answer that question normally and ignore everything below.

## Step 1 — resolve the audience

Pick exactly one audience.

**Check memory before guessing.** Crew carries a persistent user profile, and a
request like "explain this to my daughter" or "break this down for Priya" often
resolves against something already recorded — an age, a role, an interest.
Search memory and lessons for that person and use what is there; guessing an age
the profile already contradicts is the most visible way this skill fails.

If nothing resolves and no audience is named, do not silently invent one:

- Explicit smallest-audience phrasing ("dumb it down", "explain like I am")
  means **Age 5**. That is the request.
- Anything else with no audience — ask which audience in one line, or state the
  row you assumed in one clause so the user can correct it.

If the request names someone you cannot classify (a specific colleague, a title
absent from the tables), map them onto the nearest row and say which row.

### Ages

| Audience | Calibration |
|---|---|
| Age 5 | Smallest words. Analogies from toys, animals, candy, playground. One idea per sentence. |
| Age 10 | Elementary. Cause-and-effect is fine. Analogies from school, sports, video games. |
| Age 15 | Some abstraction is fine. Analogies from phones, games, social apps. Casual, never try-hard. |
| Age 20-30 | Direct and clear. Analogies from work, money, daily logistics. |
| Age 40+ | Respectful, unhurried. Analogies from home ownership, career, running a household. |

### Education level

| Audience | Calibration |
|---|---|
| 5th grade | Concrete examples, zero jargon. |
| Middle school | Introduce a term only with its definition attached. Step-by-step logic. |
| Senior high | Moderate complexity. Proper terms, each explained once. |
| College | Academic framing. Technical terms with brief context. Theory plus one application. |
| Graduate | Assume the foundation. Spend the words on nuance, trade-offs, edge cases. Be precise. |

### Job role

| Audience | They care about | Frame it as |
|---|---|---|
| Manager | Impact, timeline, risk, cost | The business outcome and the decision that is now open |
| Engineer | Mechanism, architecture, trade-offs | Implementation, performance, maintainability |
| Designer | The user's experience | Interaction, flow, accessibility, what the user perceives |
| Director | Strategy, ROI | Market position, resource allocation, the big picture |
| Product manager | User value, scope | Feature impact, what to build and what to cut |
| Colleague | Their own work | What changes for them and what they must know to collaborate |
| Support | Symptoms and remedies | How it fails, how to detect it, what to do about it |

### Relationships

| Audience | Tone | Analogy source |
|---|---|---|
| Partner | Warm, patient, conversational | Shared routines, household tasks |
| Parents | Respectful, never condescending | Technology they already use, home analogies |
| Kids | Playful, encouraging, short | Games, cartoons, animals, school |
| Friend | Casual, some humour | Pop culture, shared interests |

## Step 2 — establish the ground truth before simplifying

A simplified wrong answer is worse than no answer, and simplification is exactly
where wrong answers hide. This is the step that gets skipped.

- **Code** — read the actual files with your file and code-search tools. Do not
  explain from the identifier names. Trace what calls it and what it returns.
- **An error** — find the root cause, not the surface string. The frame that
  reports the failure is often not the one that caused it.
- **A concept** — state it once, precisely, for yourself before you soften it. If
  you cannot, you do not understand it yet.
- **An internal design or decision** — the claim and what it depends on. Search
  the knowledge library when the answer plausibly lives in a stored doc.

When the source material is large — a whole subsystem, a long log, a wide search
— delegate the reading to a sub-agent and have it return the distilled mechanism.
The explanation is short; the reading behind it does not need to sit in your
context.

If the ground truth is genuinely unknown, say so plainly at the audience's level
rather than inventing a clean story.

## Step 3 — write it

1. **What it is** — one sentence, no analogy yet.
2. **One analogy** — anchored in something this audience touches daily.
3. **The detail that matters** — only the layers this audience can use.
4. **So what** — why it matters to *them*, in their terms.

Language rules that flip with the audience:

- **Non-technical** (young, family, business): no jargon at all; define a term on
  the spot if it is unavoidable. Concrete beats abstract. Use "you".
- **Technical** (engineer, graduate): use the real terminology — omitting it
  reads as condescension. Spend the words on trade-offs and edge cases. Be brief;
  they already hold the context.
- **Business** (manager, director): lead with impact, quantify where you honestly
  can, skip mechanism unless asked, and end on the decision.

Length follows the audience: short for a child, dense for a specialist.

## Draw it when the thing has a shape

One picture really does beat a page of prose — but only when what you are
explaining *is* a shape. Ask that first, because the answer is not always yes:

| The thing you are explaining | Draw it? |
|---|---|
| A sequence, a flow, a lifecycle | **Yes** — order is what a diagram shows best |
| A hierarchy, a containment, a topology | **Yes** — nesting is hard to hold in sentences |
| A state change, or a before/after | **Yes** — put both states side by side |
| A number that moved, a share, a trend | **Yes** — one chart, not a paragraph of figures |
| A definition, a single fact, a judgement call | **No** — a box with words in it is not a diagram |
| A trade-off between two options | Usually no — the reasoning is the content, not the layout |

Scale it to the audience the same way you scale the words. For a child the
picture often *is* the explanation and the text is a caption. For a manager, one
before/after or one impact chart, never an architecture diagram. For an engineer
or a graduate, the real mechanism, drawn precisely. For a parent, draw the
analogy, not the system.

Draw the analogy as a working object, not as labelled boxes. If a cache is a
fridge, draw a fridge whose door opens onto full shelves, not a box marked
"fridge" with an arrow to a box marked "cache". When that drawing is a widget
that moves, load the `living-ui` skill for how it moves and where its words go.

What is available, in ascending cost:

| Tool | Reach for it when | What it buys |
|---|---|---|
| ` ```mermaid ` fence | a sequence, flow, state machine, hierarchy or ER | cheapest by far; renders inline, click to enlarge |
| ` ```excalidraw ` fence | the drawing should look hand-made rather than official | informal register, full colour control from the scene |
| `<mcwidget>` | quantities, a colour-coded comparison, a real chart, a before/after panel, a small interactive probe | sandboxed iframe with **Tailwind preloaded**, the dashboard theme palette as CSS variables, and Chart.js / D3 from the allowed CDNs |
| an image file via `image-authoring` | the result must outlive the chat or be pasted elsewhere | a real file you can attach or save as an artifact |

Two rules that matter more than the picture:

- **A wrong diagram is worse than wrong prose.** It reads as authoritative and it
  gets screenshotted into other people's documents. Step 2 applies with more
  force here, not less: do not draw a mechanism you have not actually traced.
- **A diagram that restates the text adds nothing.** If the caption already says
  everything the boxes say, delete one of them. The picture should carry the part
  the sentences were bad at.

### Colour it, and make every colour mean something

**The default is deliberately flat, so a plain diagram will look plain.** In chat,
mermaid is initialised with one accent seed plus greys — contrast-safe on any
theme pack, but it gives every node the same fill. Colour has to come from the
source: `classDef` for a role you reuse, `style` for a one-off.

```
flowchart LR
    classDef happy fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#16a34a,color:#14532d
    classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#dc2626,color:#7f1d1d
    classDef focus fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#78350f

    A[request] --> B{cache hit?}
    B -->|yes| C[serve instantly]:::happy
    B -->|no| D[fetch from origin]:::focus
    D -->|origin down| E[error]:::bad
```

Two rules keep that from turning into decoration:

- **A colour is a claim.** Green means this path is fine, red means it fails,
  amber means this is the part under discussion. Colour used only to look lively
  sends the reader hunting for a meaning that is not there, which is worse than
  one flat palette. If you cannot say what a colour *means*, leave the node
  default.
- **Pick values that read on light AND dark.** The same source renders under both
  themes, and the host pins mermaid's theme precisely because a theme pack can
  set an accent that disappears into the background. Mid-tone fills with a darker
  stroke and an explicit `color:` survive both; near-white and near-black fills do
  not.

Scale it like everything else: for a child colour is doing real work, separating
the parts before the labels can be read. For an engineer, colour only the two or
three nodes that carry the point. For a manager, colour the outcome, not the
machinery.

### Reach for a widget when the content is quantities or comparison

`<mcwidget>` is not only the interaction escape hatch, and it is under-used for
explanations. It is the right call whenever the honest answer is a **chart, a
colour-coded table, or two states side by side** — things markdown cannot
express. Inside one you get Tailwind with no setup, Chart.js or D3 from the
allowed CDNs, and the dashboard's own palette as CSS variables (`var(--accent)`,
`var(--ok)`, `var(--warn)`, `var(--danger)`, `var(--card)`, plus the `-subtle`
tints).

Use those variables instead of hardcoded colours so the widget matches whatever
theme the reader is on — that is why they are injected. Load the `widgets` skill
before emitting one; it carries the format rules and the full variable list. Keep
the body to a few KB and write a file instead once it grows past that.

Still prefer markdown when markdown suffices: a widget wrapping three bullet
points is overhead, not richness.

## Delivery in Crew

- **An explanation request lifts the ban on explaining, not the length bound.**
  Never flatten an Age-5 or Age-10 explanation into one clipped jargon line
  because a verbosity block says to — the register is what this skill is for, and
  every level keeps it. Length is the other axis and it stays with the active
  level: `answer_only` holds its three checks unless the user asked for depth
  (a doc, a walkthrough, in detail) — draw the shape, twelve words a sentence in
  words a child knows, cut the rest. Its word check is the Age 5 row above, and
  its own "asked why" branch is this skill's Step 3 in miniature; an explanation
  under it follows that branch as the block spells it, and borrows the
  calibration here, never a length licence beyond it.
  `ultra` and `concise`: keep the register the audience row calls for and spend
  the words there; the level bounds length, not vocabulary.
- **Persist what gets forwarded.** An explanation written for a manager, a
  director or a customer usually gets pasted somewhere else. Save it as an
  artifact so it outlives the chat scrollback and can be revised, instead of
  regenerating it next week from a different mood.

## Rules

- Never talk down. An Age-5 explanation should feel delightful, not diminishing;
  a manager explanation should leave them able to decide, not sidelined.
- For code, explain the **purpose** before the **mechanism**. Nobody needs the
  syntax before they know why the code exists.
- Ruthless simplification is allowed and often correct: the core idea at 80%
  accuracy beats a 100% accurate explanation the audience abandons. What is not
  allowed is a simplification that inverts the meaning or invents a mechanism
  that does not exist.
- Do not stack two audiences into one answer. If the user needs both, write two
  clearly labelled explanations.
- Keep the user's language, analogies included. A translated American analogy
  lands as noise — pick one from the audience's own daily life.

## Worked shapes

**"Dumb it down: what is a race condition"** — Age 5. Two children reach for the same
crayon at the same moment. Who ends up holding it depends on whose hand was
faster that second, so the picture comes out different every time you try. Nothing
is broken; the order just is not decided.

**"Explain this to my mother: why her login keeps signing her out"** — Parents.
Check memory first for what she already uses. Then: the app keeps a pass that is
deliberately short-lived, like a parking receipt that runs out, and it asks for the
password again rather than trusting an old one. Respectful, no "token", no
"session".

**"Explain to a graduate student why we picked at-least-once delivery"** — Graduate.
Use the real terms; skipping them here reads as condescension. Spend the words
where the actual content is: the duplicate-delivery obligation this pushes onto
every consumer, and why idempotency became the caller's problem rather than the
broker's.

Note the second one: the audience is a person, so the audience is looked up before
it is guessed, and the analogy is drawn from her life rather than translated from
somebody else's.

Use those variables instead of hardcoded colours so the widget matches whatever
theme the reader is on — that is why they are injected. Load the `widgets` skill
before emitting one; it carries the format rules and the full variable list. Keep
the body to a few KB and write a file instead once it grows past that.

Still prefer markdown when markdown suffices: a widget wrapping three bullet
points is overhead, not richness.

## Delivery in Crew

- **An explanation request lifts the ban on explaining, not the length bound.**
  Never flatten an Age-5 or Age-10 explanation into one clipped jargon line
  because a verbosity block says to — the register is what this skill is for, and
  every level keeps it. Length is the other axis and it stays with the active
  level: `answer_only` holds its three checks unless the user asked for depth
  (a doc, a walkthrough, in detail) — draw the shape, twelve words a sentence in
  words a child knows, cut the rest. Its word check is the Age 5 row above, and
  its own "asked why" branch is this skill's Step 3 in miniature; an explanation
  under it follows that branch as the block spells it, and borrows the
  calibration here, never a length licence beyond it.
  `ultra` and `concise`: keep the register the audience row calls for and spend
  the words there; the level bounds length, not vocabulary.
- **Persist what gets forwarded.** An explanation written for a manager, a
  director or a customer usually gets pasted somewhere else. Save it as an
  artifact so it outlives the chat scrollback and can be revised, instead of
  regenerating it next week from a different mood.

## Rules

- Never talk down. An Age-5 explanation should feel delightful, not diminishing;
  a manager explanation should leave them able to decide, not sidelined.
- For code, explain the **purpose** before the **mechanism**. Nobody needs the
  syntax before they know why the code exists.
- Ruthless simplification is allowed and often correct: the core idea at 80%
  accuracy beats a 100% accurate explanation the audience abandons. What is not
  allowed is a simplification that inverts the meaning or invents a mechanism
  that does not exist.
- Do not stack two audiences into one answer. If the user needs both, write two
  clearly labelled explanations.
- Keep the user's language, analogies included. A translated American analogy
  lands as noise — pick one from the audience's own daily life.

## Worked shapes

**"Dumb it down: what is a race condition"** — Age 5. Two children reach for the same
crayon at the same moment. Who ends up holding it depends on whose hand was
faster that second, so the picture comes out different every time you try. Nothing
is broken; the order just is not decided.

**"Explain this to my mother: why her login keeps signing her out"** — Parents.
Check memory first for what she already uses. Then: the app keeps a pass that is
deliberately short-lived, like a parking receipt that runs out, and it asks for the
password again rather than trusting an old one. Respectful, no "token", no
"session".

**"Explain to a graduate student why we picked at-least-once delivery"** — Graduate.
Use the real terms; skipping them here reads as condescension. Spend the words
where the actual content is: the duplicate-delivery obligation this pushes onto
every consumer, and why idempotency became the caller's problem rather than the
broker's.

Note the second one: the audience is a person, so the audience is looked up before
it is guessed, and the analogy is drawn from her life rather than translated from
somebody else's.
